advert.title: SPNEGO-protected page
advert.heading: A SPNEGO-protected page lives here
advert.lead: Kerberos over HTTP: RFC 4559 carries RFC 4178, which carries RFC 4121, which carries the AP-REQ.
advert.challenge: answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Negotiate to anyone who asks for it without a ticket. Your browser will most likely fail that: Chrome and Firefox use Negotiate only for hosts on an explicit allow-list, so what you will see is the 401 itself. That is the point of the debugger — it performs the handshake by hand and shows you both halves.
advert.signInHeading: And the same handshake as a sign-in
advert.signIn: performs exactly the negotiation above — same acceptor, same checks, same code — and then starts a browser session for the principal the ticket named. Past it, an OAuth 2.0 authorization request, a wsignin1.0, a SAML AuthnRequest and the admin console all complete without anybody typing anything, because every protocol here reads the one session.
advert.difference: That is the difference between the two doors, and it is the only difference: this one proves a handshake and stops, that one acts on it. It is available to every application and registered for none — a button on the sign-in screen, appAuthnMechanism: spnego on an application entry, or fedAuthnMechanism: spnego on a federation relationship.
advert.off: It is switched off right now (krb5.spnegoAuthentication), so it answers 403 and says so.
advert.knobsOwn: The three knobs below are this page’s alone: a sign-in door with a query parameter that makes it fail in an instructive way is a footgun rather than a lesson.
advert.needs: What a client needs before it can get in
advert.notInExchange: Note what is not in the exchange: the realm, the KDC, and the SPN. The client derives the SPN from the URL’s host name and finds the KDC from its own configuration, so a SPNEGO failure is usually a DNS or SPN problem that leaves no evidence on the wire at all. The SPN this service holds a key for is above; a ticket for any other name is refused with KRB_AP_ERR_NOT_US.
advert.misconfigLead: Add these to /spnego/protected to make the negotiation go wrong in one specific way — which is what this mock is for:
advert.mic: — answer with request-mic, so the mechListMIC exchange becomes mandatory and the handshake takes a second round trip.
advert.mech: — support nothing the client offers, so the negotiation ends in reject with no explanation, exactly as the protocol requires.
advert.mutual: — accept the ticket and send no AP-REP, so the client is authenticated and has proved nothing about the server.

detail.noAuthorization: This resource is protected with Negotiate. The challenge above carries no token, which is RFC 4559 section 4: the server says only that it will negotiate, and the client is expected to know the rest already.
detail.noAuthorizationWork: What the client has to work out for itself, with no help from this exchange: that the service principal name is {spn}, which realm that is in, and where that realm’s KDC is.
detail.wrongScheme: This resource speaks Negotiate. The request offered {scheme}.
detail.emptyToken: The Authorization header named Negotiate and carried nothing after it.
detail.undecodable: The bytes after Negotiate must be a SPNEGO negotiation token (RFC 4178) or a bare Kerberos GSS token (RFC 4121).
detail.offered: The client offered {count, plural, one {# mechanism} other {# mechanisms}}:
detail.noMechToken: The NegTokenInit carried a mechanism list and no mechToken, so this reply selects {mech} and asks for one: accept-incomplete. That is the round trip the “optimistic” token exists to avoid.
detail.ticketRefused: The negotiation selected Kerberos and the AP-REQ did not pass.
detail.ticketRefusedWhy: The reason is in the responseToken of the WWW-Authenticate header, as a KRB-ERROR. SPNEGO itself carries no error detail at all, so a client that reads only negState learns nothing but “no”.
detail.badMicContinuation: Computed over the DER of the MechTypeList — the SEQUENCE, not the [0] wrapper (RFC 4178 section 5).
detail.badMic: The client’s ticket was perfectly good. What failed is the integrity check over the mechanism list — so either the list was altered in transit, or the client computed the MIC over the wrong bytes. The commonest cause of the second is signing [0] MechTypeList rather than MechTypeList: two bytes, and RFC 4178 section 5 spells the distinction out because implementations kept getting it wrong.
detail.requestMic: The ticket was accepted, and this reply is request-mic: the mechanism list must be integrity protected before the context is usable. Legal only in the acceptor’s first reply (RFC 4178 section 4.2.2).
detail.requestMicAnswer: Answer with a bare NegTokenResp carrying only the mechListMIC, computed over the DER of the MechTypeList with the subkey from your Authenticator.
detail.noPending: A bare NegTokenResp arrived, but nothing here is waiting for one. A real acceptor keeps this state on the connection, which is why SPNEGO breaks behind connection-pooling proxies and on HTTP/2 in ways nothing reports.
detail.continuationNoMic: The previous reply was request-mic, so the only thing this token needed was the MIC.
rejectedNote: SPNEGO’s reject carries no reason of its own — the structure has no field for one. Everything above this line is out of band, and a real server tells you none of it.
accepted.content: This is the protected content. Getting here took a Kerberos AP-REQ inside an RFC 4121 GSS token inside an RFC 4178 negotiation inside an RFC 4559 HTTP header — four layers, of which HTTP shows you one.
accepted.bare: none — a bare Kerberos token. Accepted, but understand what it means: with no mechanism list there is nothing for a mechListMIC to protect, so none of SPNEGO’s downgrade defence applies.
accepted.mutualYes: an AP-REP is in the WWW-Authenticate header; check its echoed ctime and you have proved who answered
accepted.mutualOff: ?mutual=off is set, so nothing has proved this server is who it claims to be
